​1. The Overdraft (OD) Logic
​The speaker suggests taking a ₹90 lakh Overdraft against a ₹1 crore FD.
​The Problem: Banks typically charge 1% to 2% above the FD rate for an OD. If your FD earns 6%, your OD interest will likely be 7% or 8%, not the "7.5%" or lower rate implied to make the math work easily.
​The Risk: You are paying interest on ₹90 lakh while trying to earn a rental yield on a property. If the property remains vacant or the "brand" isn't as good as promised, you are stuck paying bank interest out of pocket.
​2. Commercial Real Estate Yields
​He suggests a 6% rental yield and 6% annual appreciation.
​Reality Check: While 6% yield is possible for prime commercial real estate, it isn't guaranteed. Furthermore, commercial property has high maintenance costs, property taxes, and long "vacancy periods" between tenants.
​Liquidity: Unlike your FD, a shop is hard to sell quickly. If you need money fast, you can't just "withdraw" a piece of the shop.
​3. The Mutual Fund "Double Dip"
​The speaker suggests taking the 6% interest from the FD and putting it into a Mutual Fund to get 12%.
​The Math: This is technically possible (this is essentially a Systematic Investment Plan or SIP funded by FD interest).
​The Flaw: If you are using the FD interest to pay for the Mutual Fund, you aren't using it to pay off the interest on the ₹90 lakh loan. He implies the rent covers the loan interest, but if the rent is 6% and the loan interest is 7.5%–8%, there is a "negative carry" (you are losing money every month).
​4. Taxation (The Missing Piece)
​This is the biggest hole in the logic:
​Income Tax: FD interest is taxed at your slab rate (which, if you have ₹1 crore, is likely 30%). So, a 6% FD really only gives you about 4.2% after-tax.
​Rental Tax: Rental income is also taxed.
​Capital Gains: When you sell the property or the Mutual Funds after 20 years, you will owe significant capital gains tax.
​Does it make sense?
​Mathematically: It’s a "best-case scenario" calculation. It assumes 100% occupancy of the shop, zero maintenance costs, constant appreciation, and ignores the tax man.
​Strategically: It is a high-risk strategy. You are "leveraging" (borrowing money to invest). If the real estate market stagnates or interest rates rise, the whole plan collapses.
​A Simpler Alternative: As you asked in your previous question, simply putting money into a diversified Mutual Fund (without the complexity of loans and shops) often yields a better "peace of mind" return.
